resources.notes: Ctrl+Paint's short videos on straight lines, fluid linework and clean lines. The point they make: a freehand straight line is a trainable motion, improved by repetition from the big joints with a quiet wrist. Watch, then do the dot-to-dot page.
Proko's six habits for line quality: a comfortable pace, follow-through past the end, ghosting the stroke first and turning the paper. Marked free when the first pass opened it.
Paid course page, listed so you know where Proko's own line lessons and warm-ups sit. Not needed for this module.

done_when.text: In a set of ten lines between dots 10 to 20 cm apart, at least seven land on both dots in one stroke

revisit.title: Dots and curves, cold
revisit.description: Place ten pairs of dots at new distances and angles and draw each line in one ghosted stroke, then five curves through three dots each. Count the lines that land on both dots and look for corrected, hairy strokes.

found-ellipses.summary: Round things seen at an angle become ellipses, and drawing a clean freehand ellipse is a motor skill that needs repetition. This module is the drill: ghosted circles, controlling how narrow an ellipse is, ellipses that fit flat squares, and ellipses stacked along an axis. Ellipses in perspective come later, in the perspective modules.
learning_outcomes: Fit an ellipse inside a flat square so it touches all four sides

resources.notes: Proko's lesson on ellipses and cylinders (14:36, marked free when the first pass opened it). Watch it for the motion and the minor axis; the cylinder part returns in the perspective modules.
A written diagnosis of common beginner faults in freehand ellipses, including the flat-bottomed ellipse that comes from a locked elbow (search-result evidence; not opened).
An open-textbook drill: a timed page of ellipses of varied sizes and angles, keeping the pencil moving past the ends (search-result evidence; not opened).

practice.title: Timed ellipse page
practice.description: Draw at least twenty ellipses of different sizes, narrowness and tilt in one ten-minute sitting. Keep the pencil moving through the ends so they stay round, and draw through each ellipse two or three times if that is how you work best.

done_when.text: On a page of twenty ellipses, at least fifteen close with rounded ends rather than points, whether drawn in one pass or drawn through two or three times
The two halves of most ellipses are roughly symmetrical about the minor axis
Asked for a narrow, a medium and a nearly round ellipse, you draw three that are clearly different and in the right order

common_mistakes: Piling up many correcting passes on one ellipse; two or three smooth passes are fine, a tangle is not

revisit.title: Ellipse ladder, cold
revisit.description: On a new axis angle, draw a row of eight ellipses from nearly round to a thin sliver, then three ellipses in hand-drawn flat squares. Check the ends, the order of narrowness and where each ellipse meets its square.

found-basic-shapes.summary: Complicated objects become drawable when you reduce them to a few simple shapes and then to simple volumes. This module covers simplifying an object into basic shapes, the difference between flat shape and form, and two cues that make a shape read as a volume: overlap and cross-contour lines that wrap around it. It ends with redrawing an object from memory as forms and checking it.
learning_outcomes: Make one form sit in front of another with a clean overlap

practice.title: Overlap stack
practice.description: Draw five simple forms (boxes, cylinders, spheres, eggs) piled so that each overlaps a neighbour. Where a form passes in front, its contour runs unbroken and cuts the one behind; add two or three cross-contour lines to each so it reads as a volume.

done_when.text: Timed, you can break a common object into basic shapes in about two minutes
On a page of five forms, every overlap reads the right way (the nearer form's contour runs unbroken) and each form has cross-contours that wrap around it

revisit.title: Object to forms, cold
revisit.description: Pick an object you have not drawn yet. In two minutes reduce it to basic shapes, then in four minutes redraw it as overlapping volumes with cross-contours, without looking back at the lesson.

obs-seeing-and-contour.summary: Beginners tend to draw a stored symbol of an eye, a hand or a shoe instead of the shapes in front of them. This module trains looking at edges and spaces: an upside-down copy, the vase and faces puzzle, then blind, modified and continuous contour drawing. Treat these as looking exercises; they train attention, and the measuring modules handle accuracy.

resources.notes: Print the template and do the vase and faces exercise once straight through before reading anything. The site explains it in terms of brain hemispheres; that explanation is not supported by brain research, so use the exercise as a looking game only (see the lesson notes).
Watch only the opening part on eyeballing and the closing self-critique tips. Leave the measuring tools for the measuring module.

practice.description: Take a simple line image, turn it upside down and copy it slowly from one side to the other, following edges and the shapes between them. Turn both the right way up and compare. This is a looking game: it makes you follow edges instead of naming parts. It is not an accuracy method; studies found upside-down copies no more accurate than upright ones.

done_when.text: You have done the vase and faces exercise and can say which part of the profile pulled you back into drawing a symbol
On a name-ban drawing you can mark at least two places where you slipped into a symbol, and redraw one of them from the object

common_mistakes: Treating upside-down copying as a way to get proportions right; use measuring and checking for that

revisit.title: Blind then modified contour, cold
revisit.description: Choose an object with overlapping parts that you have not drawn before (a tangle of cables, a plant, a pair of shoes). Do one 2-minute blind contour, then a 4-minute modified contour with glances only at junctions. Check that the line stayed connected and the overlaps read in the right order.

revisit.title: Weighted outline, cold
revisit.description: Outline one object you have not drawn before, heavier on the underside, at overlaps and on shadowed edges and lighter on lit top edges. Beside it, draw five weights of one line. Point to each heavy line and say why it is heavy.

fig-gesture-line-of-action.summary: Gesture drawing records the movement and weight of a pose in a few flowing marks before any anatomy or outline. You learn to find the line of action, see the figure as three tilting masses (head, ribcage, pelvis), and tell rhythm (curves) from tension (angles). Every later figure module builds on this skill.

@fig-gesture-line-of-action.p2.description: Before drawing, label each reference 'curves' or 'angles'. Then draw it using marks that match the label. A day later, look at the references again without your labels and see whether you would label them the same way.

done_when.text: In at least seven of ten one-minute sketches, ribcage and pelvis tilt in clearly different directions

revisit.title: Five gestures, cold
revisit.description: Open a pose site on a set you have not used and draw five one-minute gestures: line of action first, then the three tilted masses. Overlay the line of action on one reference afterwards.

@fig-timed-gesture-progression.p0.dose: 29 minutes; 12 sessions over about four weeks, any spacing

done_when.text: You have 12 session sheets photographed, each with the best and worst pose circled and one line on the most frequent error

common_mistakes: Treating the ladder as a streak to protect; a missed session is simply dropped

revisit.title: Mini ladder, cold
revisit.description: Run five 30-second poses and two 2-minute poses from a pose set you have not used, then review the sheet: circle the best and the worst pose and name the most frequent error.

obs-visual-memory.summary: Memory drawing means studying something carefully, hiding it, drawing it from memory and then comparing. It trains you to notice what matters, because you can only recall what you really looked at, and it is the bridge between drawing from observation and drawing from imagination. After a short gate it becomes a few minutes of look, cover, draw, check in most sessions.

resources.notes: Peter Han on storing and recalling structure so you can draw without reference. Useful once look, cover, draw feels routine (no price shown when the first pass looked, but not labelled free).

done_when.text: Timed, you can complete a look, cover, draw, check cycle on a simple object in under five minutes
Checked against the set-up, a memory drawing of three simple solids has the right overlaps and order of sizes, and each solid's height-to-width ratio is within about a fifth
You have run the look, cover, draw, check cycle in at least ten sessions, any spacing

revisit.title: Look, cover, draw
revisit.description: Pick an object you have not used before. Study it for 60 seconds, cover it, draw it in two minutes, then uncover it and mark every miss in a second colour.

des-ideation-and-prompts.summary: Make many fast, rough drawings to find ideas instead of one careful drawing. You use small limits so you can start within a minute, prompt lists and random generators when you have no idea, and counts instead of streaks so a missed day costs nothing. This starts the invention strand and continues as ongoing play.

resources.notes: The official Inktober prompt list: use the words as prompts any month. The list is optional and the name is trademarked for selling products, so do not post or sell under it without reading its guidelines.

practice.title: Seven-prompt mini challenge
practice.description: Choose seven prompts from any list and draw them over the next two weeks, any spacing, with a 20-minute cap each. Change format each time (full figure, close-up, environment, object) and stop when the time is up even if unfinished.

done_when.text: You have finished seven prompt drawings from one list, any spacing, each within its time cap

revisit.title: Brief in a minute
revisit.description: Without opening the module, write a three-limit brief for a subject you have never drawn, then make eight one-minute rough variations of it. Circle the strongest and write one sentence on why.

revisit.title: Chance mark to creature
revisit.description: With your eyes closed, make three quick scribbles or blots. Open your eyes and in six minutes turn one of them into a creature or a place, then write one sentence on how its parts fit together.

des-reference-visual-library.summary: A visual library is what you can draw without looking, and it grows by a cycle: collect references on one subject, study their structure, draw them from memory a day later, then check against the references and mark what failed. This module sets up that cycle, shows where to find free, reusable reference and how to record its source and licence, and turns it into a weekly habit.

resources.notes: A short blog post on what a visual library is and how to build one: collect your own photos by subject, study from life, test recall by drawing without reference, and vary the viewpoint. It is the cycle this module runs.

practice.description: Pick one category each week (chairs, boots, street lamps). Collect ten photos from a free photo site with their source and licence, make three studies of how the parts are shaped and attached, and keep them in one folder.
The day after studying an object, draw it from memory from a viewpoint you did not study, then check against the references and mark in a second colour which parts failed.

done_when.text: For two subjects you have a study page, a from-memory page drawn a day later, and the misses marked in a second colour after checking
A from-memory drawing of a studied subject gets the main proportions and the way the parts attach right when checked against the references

revisit.title: Recall a studied subject
revisit.description: Pick one subject from your library that you studied at least a week ago. Draw it from memory from a viewpoint you did not study, then open the references and mark the misses in a second colour.
